paragraphs: §1 — Abū ʿĪsā's claim entails the same self-contradiction charged against his prophetology; and the rational-cum-scriptural case that no worship is exclusive once outsiders are admitted to it

This too involves the affirmation of the prophethood of [the] Rasūl (Fasūl), and there falls upon him in it the like of what we bound upon him in that [earlier discussion]; for [the] Rasūl alleges that he is sent to the whole of creation, the black of them and the white, and that his law has abrogated every law that preceded it; and he says, concerning the Qurʾān, that what Abū ʿĪsā alleges to be from the Lord of the Worlds is not so, since he says [Qurʾān 3:85] בְּקָא׳ ג׳רַאן ("[it says] in the Qurʾān"): "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it shall never be accepted from him, and in the hereafter he is among the losers" — together with all the abuse of the Jews in which he was prolix. So Abū ʿĪsā, in his statement that the Jews are obligated to worship by what is in their hands, gives the lie to the statement of [the] Rasūl, impugns his prophethood, and invalidates his Qurʾān; so he gives the lie to himself and contradicts his own claim, beyond escape.

[2.] As for what binds him from the standpoint of reasoned inquiry, of Scripture, and of religion: it is to be said to him that we have observed that everything by which a [particular] people is singled out, of worship, may not be entered into by others than them. That is, for instance, הַכֹּהֲנִים (the priests) and the bringing-near of the offerings, with which הָרוֹן (Aaron) and his sons were singled out — it is not permitted to anyone other than them to enter into that or to perform it. So had the Creator (exalted be He) singled out every people with some worship or with some law, He would have barred others from entering it along with them, just as

He barred all creatures from drawing near with an offering or from sending up an incense-offering — since He says [Num 18:4] כבמד׳ יח׳, ד׳ וּלְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִקְרַב אִישׁ זָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא מִזֶּרַע אַהֲרֹן הוּא לְהַקְטִיר קְטֹרֶת לִפְנֵי ה׳ וגו׳ ("so that no strange man, who is not of the seed of Aaron, draw near to send up incense before the Lord"), and He also says [Isa 56:5 — read: cf. Num 18] [בישע׳ נו׳, ה׳] וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב [יוּמָת] ("and the stranger who draws near shall be put to death"). And of the same kind also is what He made obligatory upon the Levites (al-Liwāniyya), of carrying the Tabernacle and its furnishings, and barred others from that, since He says of it also [Num 1:51] בשמ׳ א׳, נא׳ וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת ("and the stranger who draws near shall be put to death"). Yet we have not seen Him bar anyone from entering into that worship by which He is worshipped, of the Torah and its ordinances; rather, a great many creatures have entered into it — that is, for instance, [Exod 12:38] בִּשְׁמֹת יב׳, ל"ח עֵרֶב רַב (the "mixed multitude") and others; and likewise the people of Gibeon, and what came to be in the days of Mordecai [Esth 8:17] באסתר ח׳, י"ז וְרַבִּים מֵעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מִתְיַהֲדִים ("and many of the peoples of the land became Jews"); and what He stipulated also in His saying [Exod 12:49] בִּשְׁמֹת יב׳, מ"ט תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָאֶזְרָח וְלַגֵּר ("one law shall be for the native and for the sojourner"), and His saying also [Num 15:15] בְּבַמִּדְ׳ טו׳, ט"ו הַקָּהָל חֻקָּה אַחַת לָכֶם וְלַגֵּר הַגָּר וגו׳ ("[the assembly] one statute for you and for the sojourner who sojourns"). Indeed, He has promised abundant reward to whoever enters into the religion and acts by the ordinances of the Torah, of the strangers and the foreigners, since He says [Isa 56:6-7] בישע׳ נו׳, ו׳-ז׳ וּבְנֵי הַנֵּכָר הַנִּלְוִים עַל ה׳ לְשָׁרְתוֹ וגו׳ ("and the sons of the foreigner who join themselves to the Lord to serve Him"), and He says [Isa 56:6] נְשָׁם׳, וְשֹׁמֵר [read: שֹׁמֵר] כָּל שֹׁמֵר שַׁבָּת מֵחַלְּלוֹ וּמַחֲזִיקִים בִּבְרִיתִי וגו׳ ("everyone who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it and holds fast to My covenant"). So since the matter is thus, it follows necessarily that all creatures in their entirety are obligated to worship by this Torah and its ordinances — none excepted from that save one who has not heard of it nor of the prophethood of Moses.

: The bab opens by binding to Abū ʿĪsā the same self-contradiction (munāqaḍa li-daʿwātih) charged at the close of Bab 13. The figure named פֿסול / פֿס (here transcribed Fasūl / Rasūl) is, on the run of the argument, "the Rasūl" — i.e., Muḥammad: Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (the 8th-c. Persian-Jewish messianic claimant whose followers, the ʿĪsawiyya / Iṣfahāniyya, held that Jesus and Muḥammad were each genuine prophets sent to their own nations) cannot consistently both affirm Muḥammad's universal mission (which abrogates all prior law) and hold that the Jews remain bound by the Torah "in their hands." The Hebrew-script tag בְּקָא׳ ג׳רַאן = bi-Qāʾ[il] al-Qurʾān / "in the Qurʾān, saying," introducing the citation of Q 3:85. Q quotes the Qurʾānic verse in Arabic. The re-OCR diff-report flags the Kraken garble of פֿסול (the "Rasūl" tag) and of קראן/ג׳רַאן at p215 — the multimodal reading restored here. : The first scriptural pillar: where worship is tribally exclusive, Scripture bars the outsider on pain of death — the priestly qurbān and incense (Num 18:4; the zar ha-qarev yumat formula) and the Levitical transport of the Tabernacle (Num 1:51). Q's pointer at the second citation reads בישע׳ ("in Isaiah") but the lemma וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת is the Numbers formula (Num 1:51 / 3:10 / 18:7); the marginal book-pointer is garbled in the witnesses (the diff-report shows the Numbers and Isaiah pointers crossing on p214), and the zar ha-qarev yumat lemma is unambiguously Pentateuchal. Rendered as Q's pointer stands, with the correction flagged. : The contrast that drives §1: by contrast with the tribally-exclusive priestly/Levitical service, the Torah admits outsiders — the ʿerev rav (Exod 12:38), the Gibeonites, the mass conversions under Mordecai (Esth 8:17) — and Scripture legislates a single law for native and sojourner (Exod 12:49; Num 15:15) and promises reward to the joining foreigner (Isa 56:6-7). Q's inference: a worship that admits all and rewards all cannot be the proprietary law of one nation; it is universally binding. The one exemption Q allows — "whoever has not heard of it nor of the prophethood of Moses" — is the standard rationalist proviso that obligation presupposes the transmission (balāgh) of the law.
§2 — [The scriptural admission of outsiders, completing the preamble's argument]
§3 — Against the "supererogation" evasion: if outsider-observance were merely voluntary, it would carry no penalty — but it does, so it is obligatory

Now, some have alleged, concerning what we have said, that reward is due to the nations for entering into the religion of the house of Israel and acting by the ordinances of the Torah not because they are obligated to worship by that, nor because that is incumbent upon them, but only because they have done it as a supererogatory grace — and that this is the counterpart of the vow (al-nadhr) and the freewill offering (al-nadba) that a person performs, donating it voluntarily without its being incumbent upon him, and is rewarded for it.

So it is said to whoever says that: when God commanded the ordinances of the Torah, did He not promise reward to whoever acts by them, and punishment to whoever opposes them and does not uphold them? There is no escape from [saying] "yes." And if that is so, and the nations have reward in performing them, it follows necessarily that they incur punishment if they oppose them — since the one who was promised reward for performing them is the very one upon whom the threat fell for disobeying them; no other [conclusion] is admissible. And if whoever of the nations opposes them incurs punishment, then it has been established
that they are obligated to worship by them, beyond escape.

: The "supererogation" (nadhr / nadba, vow / freewill-gift) evasion: an opponent grants that the nations are rewarded for Torah-observance but denies that they are obligated — observance is voluntary almsgiving, not duty. Q's reply turns on the symmetry of promise and threat (waʿd / waʿīd): the very command that promises reward for compliance threatens punishment for breach; one cannot receive the reward-side of a command without standing under its penalty-side. So if the nations can earn reward, they can incur punishment — which is just to say they are obligated. This is the standard Bahshamī taklīf structure (obligation is constituted by the conjoined waʿd wa-waʿīd); it recurs in §6 below.
§4 — The same, pressed reductio-fashion: voluntary observance would license keeping the Sabbath but not the festivals, eating maṣṣah but not fasting on Yom Kippur — which reason rejects

And it is also said to whoever says that: if the entry of the rest of the nations into the religion and their adoption of the ordinances of the Torah is a supererogation whose way is the way of the freewill-gift (al-dadd) and the voluntary donation, then it is permitted to whoever of them wishes that to adopt some [ordinances] and leave others: so he adopts the Sabbath but does not adopt the rest of the festivals; or adopts some of the festivals but does not adopt the Sabbath; or eats unleavened bread (faṭīr) for seven days but does not fast [on] the כפור (the Day of Atonement); or adopts the Feast of Pentecost (al-ʿanṣara) but does not adopt the Feast of the New Year; or adopts the Sabbath but is not circumcised; and the like of that — just as it may be permitted to one of the house of Israel to vow and donate voluntarily the fasting of a hundred days, or an offering of a hundred head of sheep, and to another to donate voluntarily the fasting of ten days or an offering of ten head of sheep, and to another the fasting of a single day and the offering of a single ewe. Then it follows from this also that it is permitted to him to adopt this Sabbath but not adopt another Sabbath, since that is a voluntary donation; and likewise that he eats unleavened bread in this [year's] seven [days] but does not adopt it in another year; and all the like of that; and likewise that he eats unleavened bread on the fifteenth day of ניסן but does not treat it as a מקרא קדש (a holy convocation), and fasts on the day of the כפור but does not desist from work — since all of that, [on this view], is merely supererogation and voluntary donation, so it is his [right] to donate voluntarily what he wishes and to leave what he wishes; and the like of that holds in all the commandments, of the [forbidden] sexual unions and the impurities and other than that. So if they allow all that we have said, the intellects bear witness to the falsity of their statement; and if they do not allow it, and reward is due only to whoever does that on the footing of the obligation-to-worship that has been laid upon him, then it is established that they are obligated to worship by all of that. And that is corroborated also by what we mentioned of His saying [Isa 56:6 + Deut 8:3, conflated] כִּי־עַל פִּי [הַדְּבָרִים] וּבְנֵי הַנֵּכָר הַנִּלְוִים עַל יְיָ לְשָׁרְתוֹ וּלְאַהֲבָה אֶת־שֵׁם יְיָ לִהְיוֹת לוֹ לַעֲבָדִים כָּל שׁוֹמֵר שַׁבָּת מֵחַלְּלוֹ וּמַחֲזִיקִים בִּבְרִיתִי ("…and the sons of the foreigner who join themselves to the Lord to serve Him and to love the name of the Lord, to be servants to Him, everyone who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it and holds fast to My covenant") — He means thereby the whole of the covenant of the Torah. So what Abū ʿĪsā said, that every people is obligated to worship by what is in their hands, is invalidated; and it is established that there has been no law for the whole of creation, from the age of Moses to the end of time, save
the law of Moses, which is the Torah.

: al-dadd (here rendered "freewill-gift"): a rare term, paired with al-tabarruʿ (voluntary donation) and synonymous in this context with nadba/nadr of §3. The OCR is secure (Arabic, not a Hebrew lemma); the sense is "what one does gratuitously, beyond duty." : The reductio: if Torah-observance by gentiles were genuinely optional, then (by the logic of the vow, where one may pledge much or little) a gentile could pick and choose among the commandments — keep the Sabbath but skip the festivals, eat maṣṣah on 15 Nisan but treat it as an ordinary workday, fast on Yom Kippur but not rest — and even keep one Sabbath while disregarding the next. Since "the intellects bear witness" that this à la carte observance is absurd, observance must be obligatory and entire, not voluntary and divisible. The clinching citation (Isa 56:6) is here prefaced by a conflated tag כִּי־עַל פִּי [הַדְּבָרִים] ("for according to [these words]," cf. Deut 8:3 / Exod 34:27); the diff-report shows the pointer-text damaged on p213, and the bracketed restoration is conjectural — the operative lemma is the Isa 56:6 "covenant" verse, glossed by Q as "the whole covenant of the Torah."
§5 — The allied error of certain Tustarī Karaites; and that "worship by reason alone" collapses into the Brahmins' denial of prophecy

And among the Tustarīs (al-Tustariyyīn) there is a group of our colleagues (aṣḥābunā) who have agreed with him in this statement in a certain respect; that is, they allege that God did not obligate the whole of creation to worship by the law of the Torah, but obligated only the house of Israel by it. These too are bound by what we bound upon Abū ʿĪsā — that if the law were proper to one people and not another, it would not be permitted for others to enter into it. And they may be asked concerning the rest of creation: are they obligated to worship by something or not? If they are not obligated, then they are left neglected — and this is what is not admissible of the Wise One (al-ḥakīm), that He should neglect His creatures and leave them in vain without an argument [laid upon them] (ḥujja). And if they are obligated, then by what are they obligated to worship? So they alleged that they are obligated to worship by what is in their intellects (bi-mā fī ʿuqūlihim). But this statement is a ladder to the annulment of prophethood and to the establishment of the doctrine of the Brahmins (al-Barāhima), who denied the messengers and alleged that people are obligated to worship by what is in their intellects.

: Q now turns on a Karaite fellow-traveller: the Tustarīs (a Karaite group associated with the Banū Sahl of Tustar) held that the Torah binds only Israel, the rest of mankind being obligated by reason alone (mā fī ʿuqūlihim). Q's reply is twofold. (a) The same exclusivity-argument applies: a law that admits outsiders cannot be Israel-proper. (b) More damagingly, "obligation by reason alone" is a sullam (ladder, slippery-slope) to the position of the Barāhima — the Indian "Brahmins" who in kalām doxography are the stock deniers of prophecy, holding that reason suffices and no messengers are needed. The al-ḥakīm lā yuhmil axiom (the Wise One does not leave His creatures suban, in vain, without an obligating ḥujja) is the Bahshamī luṭf/taklīf premise. Q's strategy is to show that the Tustarī concession, if pressed, forfeits nubuwwa itself — a position no Karaite can hold.
§6 — Why obligation requires a messenger: command and prohibition must be secured by promise and threat, which are known only by revelation (samʿ), not by reason

And all who have affirmed prophethood proceed, in establishing the messengers, by saying that, since it is established that people were created by a wise Creator (khāliq ḥakīm) who may not neglect them nor leave them without an argument [laid upon them], but must rather require of them His thanks, and demand of them His obedience, and forbid them His disobedience and the falling-short of the thanks due to Him — it was not admissible that this be otherwise than by the hand of a messenger; for command and prohibition need to be guaranteed by a promise and a threat (waʿd wa-waʿīd), and otherwise [the command] would have no [binding] aspect: for the one commanded and the one forbidden, if he be not promised and threatened, would be left to his choice — if he wished he did what he was commanded, and if he wished he did not. But when the promise falls upon obedience and the threat upon disobedience, the one commanded and the one forbidden has been bound by that, and is constrained to acceptance. And it is not admissible that the promise and the threat be known otherwise than from the standpoint of revelation (al-samʿ), to the exclusion of reason (al-ʿaql) — since we have not found for that a place in reason, and it is reached only from the standpoint of the messenger. So when this was so, we knew of necessity that God must inevitably send a messenger to His creatures, commanding them what He wills, and forbidding them, and promising them, and threatening them. So whoever allows that most of creation had no messenger sent by God to them, and were not commanded by the hand of

a prophet, nor promised nor threatened — that He did this rather to [only] a paltry band (shirdhima yasīra) — has found no proof for the establishment of prophethood, and has made it permissible for his adversary among the Brahmins, who annulled prophethood, to claim that this party's way in worshipping by what is in reason is the way of the rest of creation.

: The positive core of the bab's rational case, and a compressed statement of Q's (Bahshamī) theory of obligation. Obligation (taklīf) is constituted by command/prohibition secured by promise/threat (waʿd/waʿīd); without the sanction, a "command" leaves the agent free and so binds nothing. But promise and threat — what specifically God will reward and punish — have "no place in reason"; they are knowable only by samʿ (revelation/audition), hence only through a messenger. Therefore a wise God who does not leave His creatures "in vain" must send messengers to all. The reductio: to say God sent a messenger only to "a paltry band" (Israel) and left the rest to reason is to hand the prophecy-denying Brahmins their whole case — for the bulk of mankind would then indeed be living by reason alone. So the Tustarī/Abū-ʿĪsā position is self-undermining: it cannot affirm prophethood for Israel while denying it for the nations. Note the recurrence of the waʿd/waʿīd symmetry from §3.

§7 — God's "being pleased" by the nations' reason-worship would parallel His being pleased by Israel's Torah-worship — yet Israel is punished for adding to it, and gentiles rewarded for entering it: the asymmetry refutes the thesis

And it is said to them: is not what God obligated them [the nations] to worship by in their intellects on the footing of what God obligated the children of Israel to worship by, on the hand of Moses — in the sense that He is pleased with it from them, just as He is pleased with the children of Israel by what He obligated them to worship by, willing of them no other, just as He wills of the children of Israel none other than what He commanded them; and they have, for performing it, reward, just as the children of Israel have reward for performing what He commanded them? There is no escape from [saying] "yes" — otherwise they would not be obligated. And if that is so, then it is said: why is it, then, that the children of Israel, if they shift to other than what they were commanded — by adding to it — become not-pleasing [to God], but rather punished; whereas these [gentiles], if they wish to enter into the religion of Israel, become pleasing and rewarded?

If they say: because the children of Israel were commanded not to add, while those others were not so commanded — we say: this statement is corrupt. For if He has set up in their [the gentiles'] intellects the prohibition of, say, five things, it has not [thereby] been validly established that those five are the ones He wills of them to the exclusion of others; for had He willed that other [thing], He would have set it up in their intellects. So since He did not set that up in their intellects, and they are not included among those commanded of [something] other [by revelation], it is established that He does not will it of them; and since He does not will it [of them], the one who does it is not rewarded but punished. So when we found Him pleased with their entering into the religion of the Torah, and rewarding them for it, we knew that they are included under the obligation-to-worship by it.

: A parallelism probe: on the Tustarī view, God's "being pleased" (riḍā) with the nations' reason-worship would have to mirror His being pleased with Israel's Torah-worship — exclusive (He wills "no other"), rewardable, and obligating. The opponent must concede the parallel ("there is no escape from yes"), or else the nations are not obligated at all (collapsing back into §5). : The asymmetry that breaks the parallel: an Israelite who adds to the commanded law is punished (the prohibition of bal tosif), whereas a gentile who adds the entire Torah to his reason-worship is rewarded. The opponent's escape ("Israel was forbidden to add; the nations were not") fails on Q's own theory of reason: if the gentile's reason genuinely fixed only "five things" as God's will, then doing more would be doing what God does not will — and so would be punishable, not rewardable. Since Scripture shows God pleased and rewarding when gentiles take on the Torah, the Torah is what He wills of them — i.e., they are obligated by it. The argument exploits Q's premise (§6) that reason cannot fix the determinate content of God's will (the waʿd/waʿīd is known only by samʿ).
§8 — Scripture attests pre-Sinai obligation by non-rational law: the Canaanites were punished for the forbidden unions, a samʿī (not rational) prohibition imposed through Noah, Abraham, and Jacob

And of what Scripture indicates concerning what we have said — and that people, from of old, were obligated to worship by what is not in their intellects — is that we have seen the Maker (sublime and mighty), after He had imposed the prohibition of what He forbade of the [forbidden] degrees (al-darajāt), which is the prohibition of marriage with the close kindred, [say] by the word of the prophet to the children of Israel [Lev 18:27-28] כִּי אֶת כָּל הַתּוֹעֵבוֹת הָאֵל עָשׂוּ אַנְשֵׁי הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵיכֶם וְלֹא תָקִיא הָאָרֶץ אֶתְכֶם בְּטַמַּאֲכֶם אֹתָהּ כַּאֲשֶׁר קָאָה אֶת הַגּוֹי אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵיכֶם וג' ("for all these abominations the men of the land who were before you did … that the land not vomit you out when you defile it, as it vomited out the nation that was before you"). So He informed that He was wroth with the שבעה גוים (the seven nations) on account of their perpetration of these things which He mentioned and forbade. Now had these not been forbidden to them, and had they not been obligated to worship by [refraining from] them, He would not have called them to account nor taken vengeance on them for doing them. And these [forbidden] sexual unions which He mentioned and forbade are not of the kind that reason forbids; they were known only from the standpoint of revelation (al-samʿ). So this is among the most indicative proofs that those of the people who went before, of the שבעה גוים and others, were obligated to worship by [something] other than what is in the intellects — and that on the hands of the prophets, such as נֹחַ וְאַבְרָהָם וְיַעֲקֹב (Noah, Abraham, and Jacob) and others.

: The first scriptural argument for pre-Mosaic, non-rational obligation: Lev 18:27-28 reports that the Canaanites ("the seven nations") were punished — the land "vomited them out" — for the forbidden unions (al-darajāt, the prohibited "degrees" of kinship). Q's logic: punishment presupposes obligation; the incest-prohibitions are samʿī (revealed), not rational (reason does not, of itself, forbid e.g. aunt-marriage); therefore gentiles were under revealed, non-rational law before Sinai — transmitted through Noah, Abraham, Jacob. This both refutes "gentiles are bound by reason alone" and establishes the antiquity of universal revealed obligation. (The diff-report shows the Lev 18 lemma and the shivʿah goyim tag heavily garbled by Kraken on pp. 211-210; the multimodal text is followed.)
§9 — Sacrifice (Cain and Abel), and circumcision imposed on Abraham's seed forever, are non-rational obligations binding on the nations descended from him

That is corroborated by what we have seen of the bringing-near of קָרְבָּן וְהַכֹּל לַקָּרְבָן (an offering — and all pertaining to the offering), which has no cause in reason, and [by] God's acceptance of the offering of הֶבֶל (Abel) to the exclusion of the offering of קַיִן (Cain). So we knew from that that God (sublime and mighty) had commanded אָדָם (Adam) with that, and that it was binding upon his offspring forever. And this is very firm; and firmer than it is God's command לְאַבְרָהָם (to Abraham, peace be upon him) concerning circumcision, and His binding it upon his offspring to the end of time, since He says [Gen 17:9] בראש' יז, ט' וְאַתָּה אֶת בְּרִיתִי תִשְׁמֹר אַתָּה וְזַרְעֲךָ לְדוֹרוֹתָם ("and you shall keep My covenant, you and your seed throughout their generations"), and His saying [Gen 17:10] בסִמ', י' הִמּוֹל לָכֶם כָּל זָכָר ("every male among you shall be circumcised"). For does any doubter doubt that circumcision — which is a revealed ordinance (farīḍa samʿiyya), not a rational one, but is rather, in the view of some people, contrary to reason, since it involves the inflicting of pain upon infants, which in their view is among the things the intellects refuse and disavow — is nonetheless binding לְוַלַד יִשְׁמָעֵאל וּלְוַלַד עֵשָׂו וּלְגַמִיע וַלַד קְטוּרָה (upon the offspring of Ishmael, and the offspring of Esau, and all the offspring of Keturah)? So is it admissible
[10.] that circumcision be binding upon these nations in their entirety, yet lapse from the rest of the nations?

: קָרְבָּן וְהַכֹּל לַקָּרְבָן ("an offering, and all [that pertains] to the offering"): the bracketing phrase is Q's own (in Hebrew script), marking that he intends the whole institution of sacrifice, not a single rite. The diff-report confirms the multimodal reading of the qorban / Hevel / Qayin / Adam sequence on p210, badly mangled by Kraken. : The second and third scriptural arguments, both turning on non-rational (samʿī) institutions binding pre-Mosaic and non-Israelite lines. (a) Sacrifice: the acceptance of Abel's offering over Cain's (Gen 4) shows sacrifice was already commanded — to Adam — "with no cause in reason," and binding on his descendants. (b) Circumcision: imposed on Abraham "and your seed … throughout their generations" (Gen 17:9-10), it is the paradigm farīḍa samʿiyya — indeed one that some (the aṣḥāb al-ʿuqūl, reason-only party) deem contrary to reason (it pains infants). Yet it binds the seed of Ishmael, Esau, and Keturah — i.e., the Arab and Edomite nations. Q's pointed question (running into §10): if circumcision binds these nations by inheritance from Abraham, on what principle does it "lapse" from the rest? — undercutting the Israel-only thesis from within the opponents' own admitted cases.
§10 — The objection that the Abrahamic nations are bound only while adhering to "the whole of Abraham's law" — and Q's reply distinguishing wholesale apostasy from particular transgression
If a sayer says: circumcision is incumbent upon these nations whom I mentioned, of the offspring of Abraham, [only] when

they are upholding the whole of the law of Abraham; but if they have abandoned it and gone out from it, circumcision is not incumbent upon them — we say: thus do we [too] say; except that the whole of the law is binding upon them and incumbent upon them, [such that] if they abandon it and go out from it, they are unbelievers (kuffār) as to the whole, and are not [then] held to account for [each] single one of the ordinances. For one is held to account for the particulars (al-juzʾiyyāt), and for the falling-short in the single ordinance, the second, and the third, [only when] he is one who is upholding the whole, acknowledging it, confessing that he is in transgression, sinning in his falling-short. And likewise we say concerning the law of Moses (peace and mercy be upon him): that it is binding upon the whole of creation; so whoever adopts it and acknowledges it, its particulars become binding upon him and he is held to account for each single one of them; whereas whoever goes out from its whole is not held to account for its particulars — since we do not put to death whoever of the nations [merely] declares the Sabbath permitted, nor whoever breaks the fast on the Day of Atonement; rather we put to death [only] the Israelite, and the convert (al-dayr), who does that — the one who has entered into the whole and made it binding upon himself.

: The distinction that answers a real difficulty: if the whole law binds the Abrahamic nations, why are uncircumcised Ishmaelites not "guilty" of every infraction? Q's reply: wholesale apostasy (going out from "the whole," al-jumla) makes one a kāfir simpliciter — not liable on each particular commandment; particular liability (for breaking this or that ordinance) attaches only to one who stands within the whole, acknowledging it. Hence Karaite practice itself: a gentile who profanes the Sabbath or eats on Yom Kippur is not executed; only an Israelite — or a convert (here דיר, al-dayr, evidently a term for the proselyte who has "entered the whole") — is, because he has bound the whole upon himself. The universal bindingness of the Torah (its luzūm on all mankind) is thus compatible with the differential liability for particulars. The term al-dayr is unusual; it is read here as a designation for the proselyte/convert, on the parallel with "the Israelite."
§11 — Moses' covenant (Deut 29:13) is cut "not with you alone": it embraces those "not here," i.e., all mankind — and the idiom for "descendants" (you and your children) is deliberately not used

And of the proof also that the law of the Torah is binding upon the whole of creation is the saying of our master Moses (peace be upon him) [Deut 29:13] דבר' כט, וג' ולא אתכם לבדכם אנכי כורת את הברית הזאת ("not with you alone do I cut this covenant"), then he said [Deut 29:14] שם, [י]ד כי את אֵת אֲשֶׁר יֶשְׁנוֹ פֹּה עִמָּנוּ עוֹמֵד הַיּוֹם לִפְנֵי יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר אֵינֶנּוּ פֹּה עִמָּנוּ הַיּוֹם וג' ("but with him who is here with us standing this day before the Lord our God, and with him who is not here with us this day"). So he informed that this covenant — which is the covenant of the Torah — is not one He cuts with the house of Israel only, since they were all of them, in their entirety, present there [already]; rather, that covenant is [also] with whoever was not present there — and they are the rest of creation. So if a claimant claims that he intended thereby [only] those who would come forth from their loins after them [their descendants], [we reply that] it is not the way of Scripture to use the like of this expression for their children, nor for one who is [as yet] non-existent; for in every place where He wishes to bind [the descendants] who come forth from their loins, He says only "you and your children." That is, for instance, His saying [Deut 33:4] דבר' לג, ד' תּוֹרָה צִוָּה לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב וג' ("Moses commanded us a Torah, an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob"); and the like of that

is much. And likewise He says in many of the ordinances [Lev 23:14 etc.] חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדוֹרוֹתֵיכֶם ("a perpetual statute throughout your generations") — [so] that His saying אֶתְכֶם ("you") includes their children within it, while His saying וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר אֵינֶנּוּ פֹּה ("and him who is not here") intends others [than Israel].

: The keystone scriptural argument, from Deut 29:13-14. Moses cuts the covenant "not with you alone … but with him who is not here this day." Q reads "him who is not here" as non-Israelites — the rest of mankind — since all Israel was present, so "not here" cannot refer to them. He blocks the obvious rejoinder ("'not here' = future descendants") with a philological rule: when Scripture means descendants it uses the fixed idiom "you and your children" (or le-doroteikhem, "throughout your generations," Lev 23:14; cf. Deut 33:4 "inheritance of the congregation of Jacob"). Since that idiom is not used here, "him who is not here" must mean the spatially absent — the other nations. This is the exegetical hinge on which the universal-Torah thesis rests; §12 reinforces it.
§12 — A second construal of "him who is not here": the absent are absent elsewhere (so, living non-Israelites), not non-existent descendants; and the prophets praise the foreigner who joins

And [there is] yet another aspect also, namely His saying נִצָּבִים הַיּוֹם וְאֶת אֲשֶׁר אֵינֶנּוּ פֹּה הַיּוֹם ("[you are] standing today … and him who is not here today"). For he said "whoever is not present here" — and this indicates that he is present in another place; whereas their children, whom [the objector] wishes to have come forth from them [in the future], are present neither there nor anywhere else [since they do not yet exist]. So we knew from this that he intended only the rest of creation, who are present in other places. And again, Scripture brought out the statement in the manner of generality (makhraj ʿumūm), and did not restrict it to one people to the exclusion of another, since He says וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר אֵינֶנּוּ פֹּה ("and him who is not here"). And when that is so, it is not permitted for anyone to render it restricted save by a proof — namely that He should have barred [the others] from that in another place; yet we have not seen that, but have rather seen its contrary: the praise and the promise to whoever enters into the law, since שעיהו (Isaiah, peace be upon him) says [Isa 56:1] כֹּה אָמַר יְיָ שִׁמְרוּ מִשְׁפָּט וַעֲשׂוּ צְדָקָה כִּי קְרוֹבָה יְשׁוּעָתִי לָבוֹא וְצִדְקָתִי לְהִגָּלוֹת ("thus says the Lord: keep judgment and do righteousness, for My salvation is near to come and My righteousness to be revealed"); and he says [Isa 56:2] בְּשַׁעְיָה ב׳ אַשְׁרֵי אֱנוֹשׁ יַעֲשֶׂה זֹּאת וּבֶן אָדָם יַחֲזִיק בָּהּ שֹׁמֵר שַׁבָּת מֵחַלְּלוֹ ("happy is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it, who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it") — and his saying אֱנוֹשׁ ("man") refers back to all people. Then he says after that [Isa 56:3] בְּשַׁעְיָה ג׳ וְאַל יֹאמַר בֶּן הַנֵּכָר הַנִּלְוֶה אֶל יְיָ לֵאמֹר וגו׳ ("and let not the son of the foreigner who joins himself to the Lord say…"), and he says [Isa 56:6] בְּשַׁעְיָה ו׳ וּבְנֵי הַנֵּכָר הַנִּלְוִים עַל יְיָ לְשָׁרְתוֹ ("and the sons of the foreigner who join themselves to the Lord to serve Him"), and he said [Isa 56:7] בשעיה ז׳ וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּכָל תְּפִלָּתִי ("and I will make them joyful in all My prayer-[house]"). So he praised the foreigner who enters [into the religion] and promised him for that abundant reward; and had that been non-binding and non-incumbent upon him, he would not have been praised nor rewarded for his adopting it.

: A second reading of Deut 29:15 ("standing here today … and him who is not here today"): the verbal contrast is spatial — those "not here" are present somewhere else, hence living contemporaries (the other nations), not yet-unborn descendants (who are present nowhere). Q adds the rule that an unrestricted statement (makhraj ʿumūm) stays universal unless Scripture elsewhere restricts it — and it does the opposite, praising and rewarding the joining foreigner (the Isa 56 cluster: ashrei enosh — "enosh refers back to all mankind"; ben ha-nekhar ha-nilveh; u-vnei ha-nekhar; ve-simmaḥtim). The internal numbering "בשעיה ב/ג/ו/ז" ("in Isaiah, [verse] 2 / 3 / 6 / 7") is Q's running pointer within Isa 56, not separate chapters. Reward presupposes obligation (the §3/§6 waʿd premise), so the foreigner's observance is obligatory, not supererogatory.

§13 — Conclusion: the Torah binds all mankind from Moses to the end of days; the apparent counter-prooftext (Ps 147:19-20, "He has not done so for any nation") refutes only prophecy sent to others, not obligation — and the transition back to the Messiah-prophethood question

So the prescription of the Torah is, beyond escape, binding and incumbent upon the whole of creation in its entirety, from [the time] God sent Moses to the end of time; and whoever opposes this statement has opposed both reason and revelation (al-ʿaql wa-l-samʿ) together. Now perhaps one who clings [to a counter-text] may cling to the saying of Scripture [Ps 147:19] בתנ׳ך׳ מַגִּיד דְּבָרָיו לְיַעֲקֹב חֻקָּיו וּמִשְׁפָּטָיו לְיִשְׂרָאֵל ("He declares His words to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel"), and His saying after that [Ps 147:20] בְּתִהִלּ׳ לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי וּמִשְׁפָּטִים וְגוֹ׳ ("He has not done so for any nation, and as for judgments…"), and may fancy that this statement indicates that the Maker (sublime and mighty) did not obligate the rest of creation to worship by what He obligated the house of Israel to worship by. But this is an erroneous fancy. The meaning of it is rather that God

did not address anyone in the manner of prophecy (ʿalā jihat al-nubuwwa) from other than the house of Israel — since the prophets were from among them and not from others. That is the meaning of His saying מַגִּיד דְּבָרָיו לְיַעֲקֹב ("He declares His words to Jacob") and His saying לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי וג' ("He has not done so for any nation"). We return now to the refutation of what Abū ʿĪsā claimed, of the affirmation of the prophethood of the Messiah (מָשִׁיחַ).

: The conclusion (binding upon all "from Moses to the end of time") and the disarming of the one serious counter-prooftext. Ps 147:19-20 — "He declares His words to Jacob … He has not done so for any nation" — seems to make the law Israel-exclusive. Q's distinction: the verse concerns the medium of prophecy, not the scope of obligation. God sent prophetic address only through Israel (all the prophets were Israelite); it does not say the law thereby revealed binds Israel alone. So the universal-obligation thesis stands. The closing sentence — narjiʿu al-āna ilā ifsād mā iddaʿāhu Abū ʿĪsā min ithbāt nubuwwat al-Masīḥ — is the explicit transition: having refuted Abū ʿĪsā's every-nation-its-own-law doctrine, Q now resumes the refutation of Abū ʿĪsā's affirmation of the prophethood of "the Messiah" (i.e., of Jesus), which is the subject of Bab 15. The witnesses diverge here on the closing word: the Bab-14 file reads מָשִׁיחַ ("the Messiah," = Jesus), the Bab-15 file's parallel of the same sentence reads מֹשֶׁה (Moses); on the run of the argument — Abū ʿĪsā affirmed the prophethood of Jesus and Muḥammad to their nations — מָשִׁיחַ (Jesus) is the better reading and is followed here, with the variant noted.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is explicit: fī ifsād qawl Abī ʿĪsā anna kulla qawmin mutaʿabbidūna bi-mā fī aydīhim — "on refuting the statement of Abū ʿĪsā that every people is obligated to worship by what is in their hands." The adversary is Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (Yiṣḥaq b. Yaʿqūb Obadiah of Isfahan), the 8th-century Persian-Jewish messianic claimant whose sect, the ʿĪsawiyya / Iṣfahāniyya, uniquely among Jewish groups affirmed the genuine prophethood of both Jesus and Muḥammad — each sent, on their view, to his own nation, with the Torah remaining valid for the Jews. Bab 14 attacks the doctrinal premise that makes this possible: religious particularism — that "every people is obligated to worship by what is in their hands." Q's counter-thesis is the universality of the Torah of Moses (binding on all mankind). The bab thus belongs to Q's larger anti-ʿĪsawī sequence (Bab 13 had refuted Abū ʿĪsā's prophetology; Bab 14 his particularism; Bab 15 will resume the refutation of his affirmation of Jesus' prophethood).

- A secondary, intra-Karaite target (§5). Strikingly, Q turns the same argument against aṣḥābunā — "our [own] colleagues," specifically a group of the Tustarīs (the Karaite circle associated with the Banū Sahl al-Tustarī) — who held a milder version of the same particularism: the Torah binds Israel only, the nations being obligated by reason alone (mā fī ʿuqūlihim). Q's willingness to bind a Karaite faction with the same chain he forged for the heresiarch Abū ʿĪsā is characteristic of his even-handed rationalism; and his charge — that "obligation by reason alone" is a sullam (ladder) to the prophecy-denying Brahmins (al-Barāhima) — shows the kalām doxography of prophecy-deniers fully assimilated into Karaite polemic.

- The theory of obligation (taklīf): the spine of §§3, 6, 7. The rational half of the bab rests throughout on a single Bahshamī premise: obligation is constituted by command/prohibition secured by promise/threat (waʿd wa-waʿīd); a "command" without a sanction binds nothing, since the agent remains mukhayyar (free to comply or not). From this Q derives (a) §3: the nations cannot collect the reward-side of Torah-observance without standing under its punishment-side — i.e., they are obligated, not supererogating; (b) §6: since what God will reward/punish has "no place in reason" and is known only by samʿ (revelation), a wise God must send messengers — to all, not to "a paltry band"; (c) §7: God's "being pleased" by gentile Torah-observance, and His rewarding it, prove the Torah is what He wills of them. The whole is the Karaite deployment of ʿAbd al-Jabbār's taklīf/luṭf apparatus.

- The scriptural half (§§8–13): pre-Sinai, non-rational, universal obligation. Q's exegetical strategy is to exhibit revealed (not rational) law binding before Sinai and outside Israel: the forbidden-degree incest laws for which the Canaanites were punished (Lev 18:27-28, §8); sacrifice, commanded to Adam (Cain/Abel, §9); and circumcision, imposed on Abraham's whole seed — including the Arab and Edomite nations descended from Ishmael, Esau, and Keturah (Gen 17:9-10, §§9-10). The climax is the philological reading of Deut 29:13-14 (§§11-12): the covenant cut "not with you alone … [but with] him who is not here" must mean the other nations (living, present-elsewhere), not yet-unborn Israelite descendants — for whom Scripture reserves the fixed idiom "you and your children" / le-doroteikhem. The Isa 56 cluster (the praised, rewarded "foreigner who joins") recurs as the positive proof that gentile observance is obligatory (reward presupposing obligation).

- The karet/liability distinction (§10). A genuinely subtle move answers the obvious objection (if the Torah binds all, why are uncircumcised gentiles not "guilty" of every commandment?): universal bindingness (luzūm of "the whole," al-jumla) is distinguished from particular liability. Wholesale non-adherence makes one a kāfir simpliciter, not punishable per-commandment; per-commandment liability (and capital sanction) attaches only to one who has "entered the whole" — the Israelite or the convert (al-dayr). This both preserves the universal thesis and matches Karaite penal practice (gentiles are not executed for Sabbath-breach).

- The one counter-prooftext (§13). Ps 147:19-20 ("He declares His words to Jacob … He has not done so for any nation") is the natural particularist text; Q neutralizes it by distinguishing the medium of prophecy (Israel-exclusive — all the prophets were Israelite) from the scope of obligation (universal). The verse denies that God prophetically addressed the nations, not that the revealed law binds them.
